claim: The crystal structure of the human β2 extracellular domain was solved at 1.35Å resolution.
source: To investigate the mechanisms by which β-subunits influence Nav channel function, we solved the crystal structure of the β2 extracellular domain at 1.35Å.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution of the crystal structure in the abstract and provides crystallographic data.

claim: The hβ2 extracellular domain construct encompasses residues 30–153.
source: The construct encompasses residues 30–153 (Figure 2), and contains a single Cys mutation (C55A) to facilitate crystallization
evidence: The manuscript directly states the residue range of the construct used for crystallization.

claim: The C55A mutation was introduced to facilitate crystallization of hβ2.
source: The construct encompasses residues 30–153 (Figure 2), and contains a single Cys mutation (C55A) to facilitate crystallization [The C55A mutation is located on the protein surface and therefore unlikely to affect the overall structure (Figure 1a,d).].
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the purpose of the C55A mutation.

claim: The hβ2 configuration displays an Ig-like fold consisting of eleven β-strands and three 310 helices.
source: The hβ2 configuration displays an Ig-like fold, consisting of eleven β-strands and three 310 helices.
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the structural features observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The hβ2 extracellular domain contains four cysteines in addition to the mutated C55A.
source: Other than the mutated Cys (C55A), this domain contains four additional cysteines that are arranged in two bonds.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cysteines present in the structure.

claim: A disulfide bond between 50Cys and 127Cys is strictly conserved among all four β-subunit isoforms.
source: The first, intra-subunit bond, is strictly conserved among all four β-subunit isoforms and is mediated by 50Cys and 127Cys buried within the core where it links two opposing faces of the protein.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the conservation of this disulfide bond across isoforms.

claim: The 72Cys-75Cys disulfide bond is located within a loop that spans residues 70–77.
source: The second intra-subunit bond is located within a loop that spans residues 70–77 and connects strand β5 to β6 via 72Cys - 75Cys (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the location and residues involved in this disulfide bond.

claim: The 72Cys-75Cys loop constitutes a unique feature of hβ2 since corresponding cysteines are absent in β1, β3, and β4.
source: This loop constitutes a unique feature of hβ2 since corresponding cysteines are absent in β1, β3, and β4.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the uniqueness of this feature among β-subunit isoforms.

claim: The 72Cys-75Cys loop region displays a dual conformation in the crystal structure indicating high flexibility.
source: Remarkably, this region displays a dual conformation in the crystal structure which indicates a high degree of flexibility (Figure 1b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the observation of dual conformation and interprets it as indicating flexibility.

claim: The 72Cys-75Cys disulfide bond is highly conserved in almost all species that express β2.
source: Remarkably, this additional loop is highly conserved in almost all species that express β2, suggesting an evolutionary conserved contribution to function (see Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the conservation across species and references supporting figures.

claim: The overall hβ2 extracellular domain exhibits a similar fold compared to hβ3 and hβ4 structures.
source: Although the overall hβ2 extracellular domain exhibits a similar fold compared to that of the previously reported hβ311 and hβ49 structures, considerable differences are observed.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the structural folds of different β-subunit isoforms.

claim: At the protein sequence level, hβ2 is most closely related to hβ4 with 26% identity and 48% conservation.
source: Yet, at a protein sequence level, hβ2 is most closely related to hβ4 (26% identical; 48% conserved) (Figure 2d,e).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides sequence identity and conservation percentages.

claim: The N-terminal region of hβ2 is structured rather than disordered as in hβ4.
source: Of note is that the N-terminal region of hβ2 is structured rather than disordered in hβ4, adding an additional short β strand (β1) which interacts with the novel β4 strand.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the N-terminal structural features between hβ2 and hβ4.

claim: 55Cys in hβ2 is crucial in modulating Nav1.2 susceptibility to toxins from spider and scorpion venom.
source: We previously found that 58Cys on the surface of β4 is crucial in modulating Nav1.2 susceptibility to toxins from spider and scorpion venom (Gilchrist et al., 2013). The hβ2 subunit possesses a corresponding Cys at position 55
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the role of 55Cys based on previous findings with the corresponding residue in β4.

claim: The hβ2 subunit reduces the degree of hNav1.2 current inhibition by ProTx-II.
source: Similar to β4, we observe that the hβ2 subunit expresses abundantly and traffics to the membrane (Figure 3d) where it is able to reduce the degree of hNav1.2 current inhibition by ProTx-II.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional effect of hβ2 on ProTx-II inhibition.

claim: 100 nM ProTx-II reduces hNav1.2 conductance to approximately 17% of peak in the absence of hβ2.
source: Specifically, 100 nM ProTx-II reduces hNav1.2 conductance to ∼17% of peak whereas the current remaining in the presence of hβ2 is typically more than ∼64% of peak conductance, thereby demonstrating a protective effect.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides quantitative data on ProTx-II inhibition.

claim: In the presence of hβ2, the current remaining after 100 nM ProTx-II treatment is typically more than 64% of peak conductance.
source: Specifically, 100 nM ProTx-II reduces hNav1.2 conductance to ∼17% of peak whereas the current remaining in the presence of hβ2 is typically more than ∼64% of peak conductance, thereby demonstrating a protective effect.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides quantitative data on the protective effect of hβ2.

claim: The C55A mutation in hβ2 causes ProTx-II inhibition of hNav1.2 to resemble that of the wild-type channel without hβ2 present.
source: Indeed, the C55A mutant traffics to the membrane and causes ProTx-II inhibition of hNav1.2 to resemble that of the wild-type (WT) channel without hβ2 present (Figure 3c,d, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional consequence of the C55A mutation.

claim: The C55S mutation in hβ2 results in ProTx-II-induced hNav1.2 inhibition that is indistinguishable from that of the channel alone.
source: Moreover, the extent of ProTx-II-induced hNav1.2 inhibition in the presence of C55S is indistinguishable from that of the channel alone (Figure 3c, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional effect of the C55S mutation.

claim: 55Cys in hβ2 conveys ProTx-II protection to hNav1.2.
source: Altogether, these results support the notion that hβ2 conveys ProTx-II protection to hNav1.2 via 55Cys
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes that 55Cys is responsible for the protective effect.

claim: Loss of the covalent link between rβ2 and hNav1.1 disrupts the targeting of rβ2 to nodes of Ranvier and to the axon initial segment in hippocampal neurons.
source: Altogether, these results support the notion that hβ2 conveys ProTx-II protection to hNav1.2 via 55Cys and may relate to previous work in which the loss of the covalent link between rβ2 and hNav1.1 disrupts the targeting of rβ2 to nodes of Ranvier and to the axon initial segment in hippocampal neurons (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work describing the functional consequences of disrupting the covalent link.

claim: The C72A C75A double mutant of hβ2 is functionally indistinguishable from WT hβ2.
source: To determine if this loop regulates the gating or pharmacological influence of hβ2 on hNav1.2, we mutated 72Cys and 75Cys to Ala (C72A C75A) but found that it is functionally indistinguishable from WT hβ2 (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the functional equivalence of the mutant to wild-type.

claim: The C72A C75A mutant localizes to the oocyte membrane surface without or with hNav1.2 co-expression.
source: The C72A C75A mutant localizes to the oocyte membrane surface without or with hNav1.2 co-expression.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the localization of the mutant.

claim: The disulfide bond between 72Cys and 75Cys is not essential for folding of hβ2.
source: The lack of effect of the C72A C75A mutant on hNav1.2 function suggests that this disulfide bond is not essential for folding
evidence: The manuscript explicitly interprets the functional data to conclude about folding.

claim: Size exclusion chromatography demonstrates that the hβ2 C55A/C72A/C75A triple mutant produces monomeric protein.
source: To verify this hypothesis, we produced recombinant hβ2 extracellular domain containing three Cys mutations: C55A, C72A, and C75A. Size exclusion chromatography demonstrates that the mutant produces monomeric protein, indicating that the bond between 72Cys and 75Cys is unessential for folding (Figure 1f).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the biochemical characterization of the triple mutant.

claim: A crystal structure of the hβ2 C55A/C72A/C75A triple mutant was obtained at 1.85Å resolution.
source: Furthermore, we obtained a crystal structure of the triple mutant at 1.85Å which overlays well onto the C55A structure (Figure 1c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution of the triple mutant structure.

claim: The domain II S5-S6 pore loop has been postulated as the region responsible for forming an inter-subunit disulfide bond between particular Nav channel isoforms and β2 or β4.
source: Although previous work has postulated the involvement of the domain II (DII) S5-S6 pore loop as the region responsible for forming an inter-subunit disulfide bond between particular Nav channel isoforms and β2 or β4 (Chen et al., 2012; Gajewiak et al., 2014), the precise residue has remained elusive.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work that postulated this region's involvement.

claim: The C910S mutant of hNav1.2 loses the protective effect of hβ2 against ProTx-II.
source: When expressed without or with WT hβ2, the C910S mutant exhibits the same degree of inhibition by 100 nM ProTx-II, indicating that the protective effect of hβ2 is lost and that 910Cys is a critical residue for hβ2 binding (Figure 4a–b, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional consequence of the C910S mutation.

claim: 910Cys in hNav1.2 is a critical residue for hβ2 binding.
source: When expressed without or with WT hβ2, the C910S mutant exhibits the same degree of inhibition by 100 nM ProTx-II, indicating that the protective effect of hβ2 is lost and that 910Cys is a critical residue for hβ2 binding (Figure 4a–b, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes that 910Cys is critical for hβ2 binding based on functional data.

claim: The C918S mutant of hNav1.2 retains protection from 100 nM ProTx-II by hβ2.
source: In contrast, the C918S mutant retains protection from 100 nM ProTx-II by the β-subunit.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional effect of the C918S mutation.

claim: The C912S mutant of hNav1.2 displays a split toxin-sensitive population.
source: The C912S mutant displays a split toxin-sensitive population that is consistently observed throughout multiple oocyte batches.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the observation of a split population in the C912S mutant.

claim: The C912S C918S double mutant of hNav1.2 still has lowered toxin susceptibility in the presence of hβ2.
source: Our experiments on these double mutants show a much clearer picture wherein hβ2 only protects against ProTx-II when 910Cys is intact: the C912S C918S mutant still has lowered toxin susceptibility
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional effect of the double mutant.

claim: The C910S C912S and C910S C918S double mutants of hNav1.2 are completely inhibited by 100 nM ProTx-II, suggesting these mutants no longer bind hβ2.
source: whereas C910S C912S and C910S C918S are completely inhibited by 100 nM ProTx-II, suggesting that these mutants no longer bind hβ2 (Figure 4a–b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional effects and interprets them as loss of hβ2 binding.

claim: 910Cys is the disulfide bond partner of 55Cys in hβ2.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that 910Cys is the disulfide bond partner of 55Cys in hβ2, while 912Cys and 918Cys could form an intra-subunit bridge.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes the identity of the disulfide bond partner based on mutagenesis data.

claim: 912Cys and 918Cys in hNav1.2 could form an intra-subunit disulfide bridge.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that 910Cys is the disulfide bond partner of 55Cys in hβ2, while 912Cys and 918Cys could form an intra-subunit bridge.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes the formation of an intra-subunit bridge based on mutagenesis data.

claim: Losing the 912Cys-918Cys bond may result in the formation of a non-native bond between 910Cys and 918Cys.
source: However, it is conceivable that losing the 912Cys- 918Cys bond results in the formation of a non-native bond between 910Cys and 918Cys (Figure 4c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this possibility to explain the split population in the C912S mutant.

claim: A non-native disulfide bond between 910Cys and 912Cys may not occur in the C918S mutant because such a Cys-Val-Cys disulfide bond could be too constrained.
source: The data also indicate that a non-native disulfide bond between 910Cys and 912Cys may not occur in the C918S mutant, likely because such a Cys-Val-Cys disulfide bond could be too constrained.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this explanation based on structural constraints.

claim: Neither 912Cys nor 918Cys can compensate for the loss of 910Cys in hNav1.2 for hβ2 protection against ProTx-II.
source: Importantly, hβ2 cannot protect the C910S C918S or the C910S C912S mutants from 100 nM ProTx-II, indicating that neither 912Cys nor 918Cys can compensate for the loss of 910Cys (Figure 4c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that neither cysteine can compensate for 910Cys.

claim: WT myc-tagged rβ2 can form higher-order oligomers under non-reducing conditions.
source: It is worth noting that WT myc-tagged rβ2 can form higher-order oligomers under non-reducing conditions, which may complicate the interpretation of immunoblots (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly notes this observation from biochemical experiments.

claim: Oligomers of rβ2 disappear upon removal of 55Cys, highlighting the reactivity of this residue.
source: However, these oligomers disappear upon removal of 55Cys, further highlighting the reactivity of this residue.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the effect of removing 55Cys on oligomer formation.

claim: Myc-tagged rβ2 co-migrates with rNav1.2a under non-reducing conditions when co-expressed.
source: Notwithstanding this phenomenon, probing crude cell lysate uncovers a clear co-migration of myc-tagged rβ2 with rNav1.2a under non-reducing conditions, since co-expression yields a distinct myc-stained band above the highest rβ2 oligomer (Figure 5a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the biochemical observation of co-migration.

claim: Substitution of either 55Cys in rβ2 or 910Cys in rNav1.2a with Ser results in the loss of the covalent complex.
source: Substitution of either 55Cys in rβ2 or 910Cys in rNav1.2a with Ser results in the loss of this covalent complex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the biochemical consequence of these mutations.

claim: DTT completely abolishes the rβ2-rNav1.2a complex as well as the rβ2 oligomers.
source: Furthermore, the presence of DTT completely abolishes the rβ2-rNav1.2a complex as well as the rβ2 oligomers (Figure 5b).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the effect of DTT on the complex and oligomers.

claim: A disulfide bond forms between 910Cys in the DII S5-S6 linker of Nav1.2 and 55Cys in β2.
source: Thus, these results confirm our toxin experiments and suggest the formation of a disulfide bond between 910Cys in the DII S5-S6 linker of Nav1.2 and 55Cys in β2.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes the formation of this disulfide bond based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: WT rNav1.2a is present only when co-expressed with WT rβ2 in immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: In this experiment, we observe that WT rNav1.2a is present only when co-expressed with WT rβ2.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the results of immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Both 910Cys within the channel and 55Cys in rβ2 are required for co-immunoprecipitation.
source: Moreover, both 910Cys within the channel and 55Cys in rβ2 are required for co-immunoprecipitation, thereby pointing to their role in forming a disulfide bond between both subunits (Figure 3, Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the requirement of both cysteines for co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: rβ4 can reduce the degree of rNav1.2a current inhibition by ProTx-II.
source: Analogous to hβ2, we observe rβ4 protein production in oocytes (Figure 6c) where it is able to influence the degree of rNav1.2a current inhibition by ProTx-II.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional effect of rβ4 on ProTx-II inhibition.

claim: 100 nM ProTx-II reduces rNav1.2a conductance to approximately 22% of peak in the absence of rβ4.
source: In particular, 100 nM ProTx-II reduces rNav1.2a conductance to ∼22% of peak whereas the current remaining in the presence of rβ4 is ∼55% of peak conductance.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides quantitative data on ProTx-II inhibition of rNav1.2a.

claim: In the presence of rβ4, the current remaining after 100 nM ProTx-II treatment is approximately 55% of peak conductance.
source: In particular, 100 nM ProTx-II reduces rNav1.2a conductance to ∼22% of peak whereas the current remaining in the presence of rβ4 is ∼55% of peak conductance.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides quantitative data on the protective effect of rβ4.

claim: The presence of rβ4 no longer decreases ProTx-II efficacy in the C910S mutant of rNav1.2a.
source: In case of the C910S mutant, the presence of rβ4 no longer decreases ProTx-II efficacy (from ∼22% current inhibition to ∼17%, respectively, Figure 6—source data 1), thus illustrating the likely role of rNav1.2a 910Cys in forming a disulfide bond with rβ4 58Cys.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional consequence of the C910S mutation on rβ4 protection.

claim: 910Cys in rNav1.2a likely forms a disulfide bond with 58Cys in rβ4.
source: In case of the C910S mutant, the presence of rβ4 no longer decreases ProTx-II efficacy (from ∼22% current inhibition to ∼17%, respectively, Figure 6—source data 1), thus illustrating the likely role of rNav1.2a 910Cys in forming a disulfide bond with rβ4 58Cys.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes the likely formation of this disulfide bond based on functional data.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments indicate that rNav1.2a and rβ4 are covalently bound.
source: In concert, (co-)immunoprecipitation experiments with rNav1.2a and rβ4 expressed in oocytes indicate that both partners are covalently bound and that mutating 910Cys in the channel indeed disrupts the disulfide bond (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the biochemical evidence for covalent binding.

claim: Mutating 910Cys in rNav1.2a disrupts the disulfide bond with rβ4.
source: In concert, (co-)immunoprecipitation experiments with rNav1.2a and rβ4 expressed in oocytes indicate that both partners are covalently bound and that mutating 910Cys in the channel indeed disrupts the disulfide bond (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the mutation disrupts the disulfide bond.

claim: The cardiac hNav1.5 channel lacks the cysteine triad found in TTX-sensitive hNav channel isoforms.
source: Aligning the primary sequences of all tetrodotoxin (TTX)-sensitive hNavchannel isoforms (Nav1.1–1.7) reveals that the cardiac hNav1.5 channel lacks the cysteine triad while the flanking sequences are highly conserved (Figure 7a).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the sequence alignment results.

claim: hNav1.5 is unlikely to form a covalent bond with hβ2 unless it occurs via a distinct site.
source: Subsequently, it seems unlikely that hNav1.5 forms a covalent bond with hβ2, unless it occurs via a distinct site.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this inference based on the absence of the cysteine triad.

claim: 100 nM ProTx-II has no effects on hNav1.5 gating or protection by hβ2.
source: However, when applying 100 nM ProTx-II to hNav1.5 without and with the β-subunit, we observe no effects on gating or protection against the toxin, suggesting that hβ2 may not modulate this channel isoform (Figure 7b–e, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional results with hNav1.5.

claim: hβ2 may not modulate hNav1.5.
source: However, when applying 100 nM ProTx-II to hNav1.5 without and with the β-subunit, we observe no effects on gating or protection against the toxin, suggesting that hβ2 may not modulate this channel isoform (Figure 7b–e, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly suggests this possibility based on functional data.

claim: hNav1.8 and hNav1.9 also lack the cysteine triad and may therefore not interact with hβ2 via a disulfide bond.
source: It is worth mentioning that hNav1.8 and hNav1.9, two TTX-resistant isoforms that are evolutionary related to hNav1.5, also lack the cysteine triad and may therefore not interact with hβ2 via a disulfide bond.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly extends the inference about lack of disulfide bonding to these isoforms.

claim: ProTx-II binds to voltage-sensing domains I, II, and IV in rNav1.2a.
source: For example, the spider toxin ProTx-II (Middleton et al., 2002) binds to voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) I, II, and IV in rNav1.2a (Bosmans et al., 2008)
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work identifying ProTx-II binding sites.

claim: ProTx-II is approximately five-fold less potent when β4 is present with rNav1.2a.
source: For example, the spider toxin ProTx-II (Middleton et al., 2002) binds to voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) I, II, and IV in rNav1.2a (Bosmans et al., 2008), and is ∼five-fold less potent when β4 is present.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the change in potency in the presence of β4.

claim: Isothermal calorimetry experiments do not support the notion that ProTx-II may bind directly to β4.
source: [An intriguing concept is that ProTx-II may also bind directly to β4 (Gee et al., 1996); however, our isothermal calorimetry experiments do not support this notion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).]
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that their experimental data do not support direct binding.

claim: The tarantula toxin PaurTx3 exclusively targets VSDII.
source: A previous study in which rNav1.2a S3b-S4 paddle loops from each domain (I-IV) were transplanted into a homotetrameric Kv channel to identify the VSDs with which toxins interact (Bosmans et al., 2008), found that the tarantula toxin PaurTx3 and scorpion toxin AahII (Martin et al., 1987) exclusively target VSDII and VSDIV, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work identifying PaurTx3 binding specificity.

claim: The scorpion toxin AahII exclusively targets VSDIV.
source: A previous study in which rNav1.2a S3b-S4 paddle loops from each domain (I-IV) were transplanted into a homotetrameric Kv channel to identify the VSDs with which toxins interact (Bosmans et al., 2008), found that the tarantula toxin PaurTx3 and scorpion toxin AahII (Martin et al., 1987) exclusively target VSDII and VSDIV, respectively.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work identifying AahII binding specificity.

claim: ProTx-I and ProTx-II both interact with the voltage sensor in DII and DIV.
source: In addition, the tarantula toxins ProTx-I and ProTx-II both interact with the voltage sensor in DII and DIV, whereas ProTx-II also binds to DI with high affinity.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on toxin binding sites.

claim: ProTx-II also binds to DI with high affinity.
source: In addition, the tarantula toxins ProTx-I and ProTx-II both interact with the voltage sensor in DII and DIV, whereas ProTx-II also binds to DI with high affinity.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on ProTx-II binding to DI.

claim: No significant difference is observed in PaurTx3, AahII, or ProTx-I effect on hNav1.2 without and with hβ2.
source: Aside from ProTx-II, we observe no significant difference in PaurTx3, AahII, or ProTx-I effect which suggests that hβ2 does not impede binding of these toxins to VSDII and VSDIV (Figure 8b–c, Figure 8—source data 1 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the functional results with these toxins.

claim: hβ2 does not impede binding of PaurTx3, AahII, or ProTx-I to VSDII and VSDIV.
source: Aside from ProTx-II, we observe no significant difference in PaurTx3, AahII, or ProTx-I effect which suggests that hβ2 does not impede binding of these toxins to VSDII and VSDIV (Figure 8b–c, Figure 8—source data 1 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly interprets the functional data to conclude about toxin binding.

claim: hβ2 primarily influences VSDI.
source: Therefore, we speculate that hβ2 primarily influences VSDI and as such, is located near this region (Figure 8d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly speculates about hβ2's primary influence based on toxin data.

claim: μO§-conotoxin GVIIJ function is influenced by hβ2.
source: Since μO§-conotoxin GVIIJ function is also influenced by hβ2 (Gajewiak et al., 2014), it will be interesting to investigate a possible VSDI binding site for this toxin.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work showing GVIIJ function is influenced by hβ2.

claim: Bacterial Nav channels exhibit a domain-swapped architecture in which the S1-S4 VSD within one subunit is located adjacent to the S5-S6 segments of the next subunit.
source: One important observation from bacterial Nav channel crystal structures (Payandeh et al., 2012; Payandeh et al., 2011; Shaya et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012) is the domain-swapped architecture of the channel in which the S1-S4 VSD within one subunit is located adjacent to the S5-S6 segments of the next subunit.
evidence: The manuscript cites bacterial Nav channel structures to describe the domain-swapped architecture.

claim: A structural clockwise arrangement has been consistently observed in prokaryotic and mammalian Kv channels.
source: Such a structural clockwise arrangement has also been consistently observed in prokaryotic and mammalian Kv channels (Long et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kv channel structures to support the clockwise arrangement.

claim: hNav channels may be organized in a similar domain-swapped fashion as bacterial Nav channels.
source: Since hNav channels may be organized in a similar fashion, the determinants of hβ2-subunit sensitivity can be located in multiple Nav channel domains.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly suggests this possibility based on structural knowledge of bacterial channels.

claim: hβ2 binds to 910Cys in the S5-S6 loop of DII and influences ProTx-II interaction with VSDI.
source: For example, we found that hβ2 binds to 910Cys in the S5-S6 loop of DII and influences ProTx-II interaction with VSDI.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly summarizes the key findings about hβ2 binding and functional effects.

claim: hβ2 may be positioned in the cleft between VSDIV and VSDI or VSDI and VSDII.
source: Although it is challenging to pinpoint its precise location, our data suggest that hβ2 is positioned in the cleft between VSDIV and VSDI or VSDI and VSDII where it is presented with an opportunity to interact with both determinants to influence ProTx-II action (Figure 8d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly suggests possible locations for hβ2 based on the data.

claim: Nav channel fast inactivation and voltage-dependence of activation changes substantially when co-expressed with the β1-subunit in heterologous systems.
source: In contrast, the consistent picture emerging from the literature is that Nav channel fast inactivation and voltage-dependence of activation changes substantially when co-expressed with the β1-subunit in heterologous systems (Chen and Cannon, 1995; McCormick et al., 1998; Qu et al., 1999; Isom et al., 1995b).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies describing β1-subunit effects on Nav channels.

claim: VSDIV plays a pivotal role in channel fast inactivation.
source: Given the pivotal role of VSDIV in channel fast inactivation (Bosmans et al., 2008; Capes et al., 2013; Chanda and Bezanilla, 2002; Horn et al., 2000; Sheets et al., 1999), β1 may be positioned close to VSDIV
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting the role of VSDIV in fast inactivation.

claim: β1 may be positioned close to VSDIV where it can also interact with the extracellular S5-S6 pore-loop within DI.
source: Given the pivotal role of VSDIV in channel fast inactivation (Bosmans et al., 2008; Capes et al., 2013; Chanda and Bezanilla, 2002; Horn et al., 2000; Sheets et al., 1999), β1 may be positioned close to VSDIV where it can also interact with the extracellular S5-S6 pore-loop within DI (Figure 8d), a presumed interacting region (Qu et al., 1999; Makita et al., 1996).
evidence: The manuscript proposes a location for β1 based on functional data and cites supporting studies.

claim: Particular Nav channel isoforms can interact simultaneously with a β1- and β2-subunit.
source: Altogether, this model suggests that particular Nav channel isoforms can interact simultaneously with a β1- and β2-subunit (Calhoun and Isom, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this model and cites supporting literature.

claim: β2 and β4 form a disulfide bond with an unidentified Cys within particular Nav channel isoforms.
source: Of the four known β-subunits and their splice variants (β1–4; gene names Scn1b-Scn4b) (Isom et al., 1992; Isom et al., 1995a; Morgan et al., 2000; Patino, 2011; Yu, 2003), β2 and β4 form a disulfide bond with an unidentified Cys within particular Nav channel isoforms.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous literature describing the disulfide bond formation.

claim: Non-covalent interactions underlie β1 and β3 association with Nav channels.
source: In contrast, non-covalent interactions underlie β1 and β3 association with Nav channels as well as other members of the voltage-gated ion channel family (Calhoun and Isom, 2014; Namadurai et al., 2015; Marionneau, 2012; Nguyen et al., 2012; Deschenes et al., 2008).

claim: Aberrant behavior of β2 and β4 subunits has been linked to long-QT syndrome, atrial fibrillation, sudden infant death syndrome, and epilepsy.
